present.d: Only text supports Present in the paper. It is used to add context that is not contained in the chart data, such as events, explanation, or narrative framing.

identify.d: All seven annotation types support Identify. Use it when the goal is to direct attention to a specific point, group, region, or time.

summarize.d: Text, glyphs, and indicators support Summarize. These annotations help readers read an overall trend, statistic, or high level takeaway.

compare.d: Enclosure, connector, text, glyph, color, and indicator support Compare. They help readers judge differences between values, groups, or trends.

enclosure.d: Closed boundaries such as rectangles, ellipses, and brackets. They isolate or group chart marks and often work with text or connectors.

connector.d: Lines or arrows that link an annotation to the mark it refers to. They reduce ambiguity and usually appear with text.

text.d: Words or sentences used for labels, descriptions, summaries, or added context. Text appears in 1,434 of 1,888 charts and is the only type that supports Present.

glyph.d: Symbols or shapes that mark points, events, or categories. The paper shows them most often in maps and line charts.

color.d: Added color used as an annotation layer to highlight or distinguish marks. Color that is already part of the chart encoding does not count as an annotation.

indicator.d: Reference lines and overlays used for trends, thresholds, averages, or correlations. Many indicator annotations are derived from the underlying data.

geometric.d: Spatial modifications such as zoom boxes or exploded slices that focus attention on one area. This type is rare and only supports Identify in the paper.

CS.label: Case 1: The Economist (Deaths of Despair)
CS.imageAlt: Case study figure from The Economist showing deaths of despair trends with annotation overlays
CS.figureNote: Cropped from the paper's Case Study 1 figure (The Economist example).
CS.desc: The paper uses this line chart to show how annotations can mark a key event, summarize trend change, and compare periods in a time series.

rows.note: Look for the vertical line and label that mark the introduction of OxyContin. This turns one year into a clear reference point on the timeline.
Look for the projected guide line and the nearby text. The line extends the earlier downward trend so readers can see where the observed series breaks from it.
Look for the colored enclosed region and label that separate one period from another. This helps readers compare how the trend changes across phases.
Look for the text callout connected to the line. The connector shows exactly which part of the trend the comparison refers to.

takeaways: One event marker anchors the timeline.
Indicator and text together show how the trend changes after that event.
Color, enclosure, and connector callouts support comparison across periods.

CS.label: Case 2: Wall Street Journal (Inflation)
CS.imageAlt: Case study figure from Wall Street Journal showing inflation bars and annotation callouts
CS.figureNote: Cropped from the paper's Case Study 2 figure (WSJ inflation example).
CS.desc: The paper uses this waterfall chart to show how annotations can make a threshold visible and connect article context to specific bars.

rows.note: Look for the highlighted enclosed area and the text that marks the 2% threshold. This shows which values fall below the target.
Look for the callout text and connector lines attached to specific bars. They add article context and make it clear which bars the explanation refers to.

takeaways: The threshold is made explicit with color, enclosure, and text.
Connector callouts add context without leaving the bars ambiguous.
All annotations in this case come from external context.

CS.label: Case 3: Washington Post (COVID-19 Peaks)
CS.imageAlt: Case study figure from Washington Post showing COVID cases deaths and hospitalization waves with annotations
CS.figureNote: Cropped from the paper's Case Study 3 figure (Washington Post COVID-19 example).
CS.desc: The paper uses this line chart to show how annotations can mark COVID-19 wave peaks and add context about cases, hospitalizations, and deaths.

rows.note: Look for the colored enclosed regions and labels around the peaks. They mark the different COVID-19 waves so readers can find them quickly.
Look for the text callouts and arrows attached to the peaks. The callouts add article context, and some of the numbers come directly from the chart data.

takeaways: Wave labels help readers separate overlapping peaks.
Connector callouts tie article context to specific points in the lines.
This case mixes external explanation with some internal values.
